title: New Economy Skills: Skills for the Maker Economy
gist: The World Economic Forum's third New Economy Skills report argues that the build-out of AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and infrastructure renewal is creating strong demand for hands-on 'maker' skills (build, operate, maintain, repair, produce), and that the maker skills pipeline is not prepared for the scale, pace or complexity of that demand. It frames the fix around three challenges: adapting to changing skill requirements, attracting more people into maker careers, and making maker skills easier to assess, recognize and credential.

insights.claim: The acceleration of AI, clean energy, advanced manufacturing and infrastructure renewal is generating strong demand for practical, hands-on skills to build, operate, maintain, repair and produce the physical goods and systems economies depend on.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: The AI and energy-transition capex cycle has a physical-labor bottleneck; skilled-trades availability is a variable to watch for data-center, grid and factory project timelines and costs.

insights.claim: The World Economic Forum argues that maker skills (hands-on build, operate, maintain and repair capabilities) are becoming a strategic advantage for both national economies and individual businesses, not merely a labor-supply issue.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Companies and countries with deep skilled-trades pools may execute physical build-outs faster; workforce access becomes a competitive differentiator in capex-heavy sectors.
insights.quote: maker skills are becoming a strategic advantage for economies and businesses

insights.claim: Based on its analysis of global supply and demand trends, the World Economic Forum finds that the maker skills pipeline is not yet prepared for the scale, pace or complexity of current and future demand.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: A persistent skilled-trades shortage implies wage inflation and execution delays for AI infrastructure, grid and manufacturing projects; a tailwind for vocational training, automation and labor-saving construction tech.
insights.quote: the maker skills pipeline is not yet prepared for the scale, pace or complexity of current and future demand

insights.claim: The World Economic Forum frames the maker-skills gap around three challenges: adapting to changing skill requirements, attracting more people into maker careers, and making maker skills easier to assess, recognize and credential.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Points to policy and spending priorities in vocational training, apprenticeships and skills-credentialing, a potential demand pocket for workforce-development and assessment providers.

insights.claim: A key bottleneck in the maker workforce is not only headcount but that hands-on skills are hard to assess, recognize and credential, which limits labor mobility and hiring into maker roles.
insights.speaker: World Economic Forum
insights.so_what: Skills-based hiring and portable credentials for trades could widen the usable labor pool faster than training new entrants; watch for credentialing standards in energy and manufacturing.
